Vest, on a mission to bring wider access to financial derivatives and other institutional investment strategies, manages investment products worth $50+ billion (as of 9/30/25). Backed by private equity, the firm has a strategic partnership with Cboe Global Markets, Inc. (NASDAQ: CBOE), and First Trust, a global asset manager.

Then, we provide automated testing infrastructure: run complex sessions against your MCPs/CLIs across all major harnesses and models to catch broken workflows before your users do.

Finally, our MCP lets your internal coding agents plug into Armature to autonomously fix your product's AX based on our run data.

The next step is to provide the foundational infrastructure for the Agent Experience, powering agent-native revenue, lifecycle marketing, and customer support for the next generation of software.

long_description.before:
Exosat is building a sovereign alternative to Starlink by mass manufacturing thousands of satellites that work as cell towers in space. By designing our architecture with zero U.S-origin parts and manufacturing with overseas partners, our satellites can be built at under a tenth of the usual cost and launched from any nation to bypass bottlenecks in launch capacity.

We're starting off by selling connectivity to OEMs and network operators, but will eventually use the distributed compute across our satellite constellation to support sovereign AI use cases as well.

We've already signed $400M+ in LOIs to work with operators across Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East, booked our first satellite launch next year, and hold an 11,000 satellite filing with the ITU to build the largest comms network outside of the U.S. and China.
long_description.after:
Exosat is building thousands of low-cost communication satellites to provide a neutral, sovereign alternative to Starlink. By building our satellites with zero ITAR/EAR-controlled content, we can leverage manufacturers anywhere in the world to produce our satellites at under a tenth of the cost and launch them from any nation to bypass launch capacity bottlenecks.

We're starting off by selling connectivity to device OEMs and network operators, but will eventually use the distributed compute across our constellation to run low-latency inference for robots and autonomous vehicles in remote and rural areas anywhere on the planet.

We've already signed $400M+ in LOIs to work with operators across Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East, booked our first satellite launch next year, and hold an 11,000 satellite filing with the ITU to build the largest comms network outside of the U.S. and China.

long_description.before: Almanac is a self-updating wiki for your coding agents. It turns your team’s AI coding conversations into connected Markdown docs that live inside your repo. Your agents automatically search the wiki before making changes, so every agent working on the codebase starts with the same context, decisions, and implementation history.
long_description.after: Almanac is Hermes with a company brain. You message it in Slack or iMessage; it knows what is happening across your company and can use your accounts to get real tasks done for you. It has a full computer, browser and terminal. It takes your Gmail, Calendar, Attio, GitHub, AI convos, docs and meeting notes and compiles them into a Wiki that keeps itself up to date. It keeps a current understanding of what you’re building, who your customers are, what was decided, and what still needs to happen. It can use websites, run code, create files and take actions across your accounts. If it reaches a login, payment or decision it shouldn’t make alone, it pings you or hands you the live browser.

one_liner.before: Self updating wiki for your coding agents
one_liner.after: The AI that knows your company

long_description.before:
Osseus is the intelligent development platform for robotics. It plugs into the tools a team already uses - CAD, ECAD, GitHub, Jira, docs, messaging, and test runs to build a live map of their robot stack: every part, board, requirement, test, and decision, and how they all depend on each other.

When a hardware change is made, the map traces the downstream impact across mechanical, electrical, and software. Osseus's agents find which requirements may be compromised, run the attached tests and sims, create fixes of the affected hardware/software on branches, and re-run the tests to confirm the design still conforms.

Osseus includes a robotics component marketplace. Teams can list spare parts and hardware for others to rent during prototyping, and designs can be evaluated against real component availability. If a part has a long lead time or is unavailable, engineers can quickly find compatible alternatives from the marketplace instead of waiting weeks or asking around their network.

Design review also happens in Osseus. Engineers see why a design might not work, what's been tried before, and why something was built the way it was, pulled from prior conversations between engineers and with suppliers. Suppliers comment directly on a part through a secure link instead of back and forth over email, and what they say is remembered. If a supplier flags that a design isn't machinable, or that changing a feature would cut cost, that insight automatically appears the next time someone designs something similar, saving time and money.

Our long-term goal is for any professional team or hobbyist to import, fork, or create a robot in Osseus. Builders will be able to explore compatible components and supplier intelligence, edit the physical design, and receive proposed updates to the robot description, firmware, control software, simulation, and tests. We ultimately want to develop physical-AI models that reason jointly over the robot's geometry, electronics, kinematics, components, software, and real-world performance so people can optimize and iterate on robots much faster.
long_description.after:
Osseus is the intelligent development platform for robotics. It plugs into the tools a team already uses - CAD, ECAD, GitHub, Jira, docs, messaging, and test runs - creating a live dependency graph of their entire robot stack. It automatically builds and maintains the relationships between every part, board, requirement, test, and decision.

When a hardware change is made, the map traces the downstream impact across mechanical, electrical, and software. Osseus's agents find which requirements may be compromised, run the attached tests and sims, create fixes for the affected hardware/software on branches, and re-run the tests to confirm the new design doesn’t break downstream.

Osseus includes a robotics component marketplace. Teams can list spare parts and hardware for others to buy/rent during prototyping, and designs can be evaluated against real component availability. If a part has a long lead time or is unavailable, engineers can quickly find compatible alternatives in their area instead of waiting weeks or asking around their network.

Design review also happens in Osseus. Engineers see why a design might not work, what's been tried before, and why something was built the way it was, pulled from prior conversations between engineers and with suppliers. Suppliers comment directly on a part through a secure link instead of back and forth over email, and what they say is remembered. If a supplier flags that a design isn't machinable, or that changing a feature would cut cost, that insight automatically appears the next time someone designs something similar, saving time and money.

We ultimately will use the platform's deep engineering understanding to develop physical-AI models that reason jointly over the robot's geometry, electronics, kinematics, components, software, and real-world performance so people can optimize and iterate on robots much faster.
